units.en: A dynamic counterpart to ⟦0⟧, weather can affect movement and combat of all types of units. Weather has a big impact on logistics and how one is able to supply units. It should be noted provinces do not always have weather, and some provinces have no temperature modifiers.

The game simulates full day-night cycles for every province on the map every hour. Over the course of a year, every province will have roughly 12 hours of daytime and 12 hours of nighttime per day, though the amount of daytime and nighttime that a province receives per day can vary depending on the day of the year. Provinces closer to the Equator will have little variance in their daytime and nighttime hours over the course of a year, whereas provinces closer to the poles can experience months with large amounts of daytime during their summer seasons and months with large amounts of nighttime during their winter seasons.
Nighttime confers the following effects to units located in it:

These penalties can be offset by modifiers that are explicitly stated as night penalty reductions, e.g., from ⟦0⟧ or a ⟦1⟧. Land Night Attack bonuses, e.g., from ⟦2⟧ or ⟦3⟧, also negate the base penalty to land attack at nighttime instead of just adding land attack at night, which is an important difference to consider when multiple sources of this bonus are applied.
Night Operations Chief of Air Force

It should be noted that carrier aircraft are affected both by nighttime penalties to their aerial mission as well as by night penalties to the carriers off of which they are based. Nighttime penalty reductions to aircraft alone are therefore far less effective on carrier aircraft unless also accompanied by nighttime penalty reductions to carriers.
Temperature plays a very important role in the game's weather systems.

Temperature is tracked for every province on the map and updated regularly. Every update tick, the temperature of a province can change up to 6 degrees Celsius,⟦0⟧ though both temperature changes and temperatures as a whole are smoothed between neighboring provinces to be more gradual overall.⟦1⟧

All ⟦0⟧ have pre-defined temperature ranges that their provinces are allowed to have at on any given day of the year. Some can have very large ranges of temperatures throughout the year (e.g., temperatures in Manchuria can range between -25 and 31 degrees throughout the year)⟦1⟧, while others can have fairly stable temperatures that are temperature throughout the entire year (e.g., temperatures in Southern England can range between -5 and 25 degrees throughout the year)⟦2⟧. Similarly, some regions can tend to have very high temperatures (e.g., temperatures in South Indochina can range between 16 and 36 degrees throughout the year)⟦3⟧, while others can tend to have very low temperatures (e.g., provinces in Northern Norway can range between -23 and 18 degrees throughout the year)⟦4⟧.

Attrition from weather only applies if controller is at war.

While winter attrition can be reduced by appointing the armies to a commander with a ⟦0⟧ trait, there is no corresponding trait to reduce heat attrition. Commanders gain the ⟦1⟧ trait by fighting for a longer time in cold weather. ⟦2⟧ has a unique focus ⟦3⟧ reducing heat attrition.

Negative effects from these modifiers can be reduced by up to 50% (at best halved) through acclimatization. Effects from ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ can be reduced with hot acclimatization, and effects from ⟦2⟧ and ⟦3⟧ can be reduced with cold acclimatization. Units gain hot acclimatization by spending time in provinces with ⟦4⟧ or ⟦5⟧. Units gain cold by spending time in provinces with ⟦6⟧, ⟦7⟧, ⟦8⟧, ⟦9⟧, ⟦10⟧, and/or ⟦11⟧. Acclimatization speed is increased by ⟦12⟧⟦13⟧ when a unit is in combat, and it can also be increased through various sources of acclimatization factor bonuses, e.g., the ⟦14⟧ commander trait or the ⟦15⟧ special forces doctrine. Acclimatization decays over time when a unit is not in a province with a modifier that would benefit from it. It also decays at ⟦16⟧ speed⟦17⟧ when a unit with cold acclimatization is in a province where it would benefit from hot acclimatization or vice versa.
Temperature Impacts on Weather Events and Modifiers

While the likelihood of weather events such as ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧, and ⟦3⟧ and modifiers representing their long-term effects like ⟦4⟧, ⟦5⟧, and ⟦6⟧ are primarily defined though ⟦7⟧ for each month of the year, temperature can also have an indirect effect in the following ways:

⟦0⟧: The rate at which collected water in a province evaporates increases linearly from 2 degrees to 38 degrees, which means mud dries out quicker at hotter temperatures. The modifier also disappears at temperatures of -1 degree or colder, as the mud freezes.

⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧, and ⟦3⟧: Snow can only fall on a province when it is 1 degree or colder, and the rate of snowfall for ⟦4⟧ and ⟦5⟧ increases linearly until -4 degrees before capping out. Snow only starts melting into in provinces at 0 degrees or warmer (snowmelt will become collected water), and the rate of snowmelt increases linearly until 12 degrees before capping out.

⟦0⟧: This modifier can only be applied to eligible sea zones when they are between 0 and -5 degrees. Once applied, they also can only be removed once the given sea zone is between 1 and 5 degrees. Some sea zones, e.g. the Bering Sea, will always have this modifier applied, while others, e.g. the Denmark Strait, might only have it applied during colder, winter months.
Weather events spawn modifiers that can have an impact on single provinces and/or entire states.

High levels of ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ will affect unit movement speed and greatly hinder the power of any offensive. These debuffs stack on top of those of ⟦2⟧ and ⟦3⟧, so smart players should be mindful of launching winter offensives in colder climates without adequate preparation, including the potential use of ⟦4⟧ with ⟦5⟧. ⟦6⟧ will increase attrition levels, especially for supply trucks used for motorized supply, and can similarly grind offensives to a halt.

If the area is set up as being susceptible to mud during a particular time of year, and the water level over a time period is high enough, mud develops. ⟦0⟧, a ⟦1⟧, or even melting ⟦2⟧ can be the source of the water. The game logs how much water is collected in each province based on past precipitation and temperature. Higher levels of ⟦3⟧ will reduce the growth of mud in a province by up to ⟦4⟧.

Temperature affects how quickly collected snow and water disappear from each province. ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ in provinces with temperatures at or above 0 degrees will melt into collected water, with melting speed increasing linearly with temperature until it caps out at 12 degrees. Collected water (that could produce ⟦2⟧) will start to evaporate at temperatures of 2 degrees or warmer. Evaporation speed increases linearly with temperature until it caps out at 38 degrees, though any precipitation in the meantime can refill provinces' collected water. ⟦3⟧ in provinces with temperatures of -1 degrees or colder will also freeze, negating its effects until temperatures become warm enough to thaw it out.

Wise players will try to avoid launching major offensives during the mud seasons of a given location. In places like the Western ⟦0⟧ and the Northeastern ⟦1⟧, this happens during the spring, when cold and snowy winters are followed by a wet and mild spring, as well as in the late autumn, when heavy rainfall and low temperatures cause a buildup of unevaporated water. In Northern ⟦2⟧ and the Southern ⟦3⟧, this can happen during mild but very wet winters when temperatures are not cold enough to cause mud to freeze, but also not warm enough for the buildup of water to evaporate, especially in areas with less ⟦4⟧.
Some terrain makes it more or less likely for a weather event to occur and/or for province modifiers from collected water and/or snow to appear.
⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧ Increases the supply use of a division in a state or province experiencing that weather. ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧ Reduces the rate that supplies flow into a province in the state experiencing that weather.
